set.text: When Amara opened a small bakery on Pine Street, she had a tight budget. She could not buy new ovens, so she used two old ones from her aunt. Every morning she baked fresh bread before the sun came up. At first, few people came in. Then a teacher from the school across the street began to purchase a loaf every day. She started to recommend the bakery to the parents at her school. Slowly the line at the door grew longer. For the first six months, Amara made no profit at all, because flour and rent cost so much. Eventually, after almost a year, she earned enough to pay herself a small wage and hire a helper.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “budget” mean?
options: a large amount of money saved in a bank
a plan for how much money she could spend
a loan she had to pay back
a list of the breads she would bake
qs.why: A budget is a plan for spending money; a “tight” budget means she had little to spend. “Cheap” is a different use of budget as an adjective, not the meaning here.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “Eventually” mean?
options: at a later time, after a long wait
qs.why: Eventually means at some later time after a long wait; here it came “after almost a year.” It does not mean “perhaps.”

qs.q: Why did Amara make no profit in the first six months?
options: Nobody ever came into the bakery
She gave all her bread away for free
Her costs for flour and rent were high
She paid a helper too much
qs.why: The passage says she made no profit “because flour and rent cost so much.” She hired a helper only later, after almost a year.

why: Text implied the teacher was a parent ('the other parents'); reworded.

set.text: Last month, Kwame decided to apply for a job as a manager at a sports store. He was one of eight candidates, and some of them had more experience than he did. To prepare, he read about the company and practiced answers with his sister. In the interview, they asked about his background. He explained that he grew up helping in his father's shop and later studied business at night. He spoke with confidence, and he was also frank: he said he had never led a team before, but he was ready to learn. Two days later, the company called to offer him the job. They liked that he told the truth.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “candidates” mean?
options: workers who already had jobs at the store
people trying to be chosen for the job
people trying to win an election
qs.why: Here candidates are the eight people competing for the manager job. The word can also be used for elections, but there is no election in this story.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “frank” mean?
options: honest and direct, even about something not nice to hear
qs.why: Being frank means saying the truth directly. Kwame openly said he had never led a team, which did not make him look good.

qs.q: What does the passage suggest was a main reason Kwame got the job?
options: He had more experience than everyone else
His father owned the sports store
He had led many teams before
The company liked his honesty about what he had not done
His sister worked at the company
He was the only person who applied
qs.why: The last line says “They liked that he told the truth.” Other candidates had more experience, so that was not the reason.

why: Removed clumsy double 'but' in one sentence.

set.text: Last spring, a small town wanted to know how to use an empty lot near the train station. The town office sent a short survey to every home, with five questions. More than two thousand people answered. A clear majority, about sixty percent, said they would prefer a park to a parking lot. Many people also wrote their own suggestions. One child asked for a place to ride skateboards, and an older man wanted benches in the shade. The people who wanted parking were mainly those who drove to the station every day. The overall result was clear: most of the town wanted green space.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “majority” mean?
options: more than half of the people
the people who drove to the station
qs.why: A majority is more than half; here about sixty percent of the people who answered.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mainly” mean?
qs.why: Mainly means mostly. Most of the people who wanted parking drove to the station, but not necessarily every one of them.

qs.q: What did the survey show most people wanted?
options: A park on the empty lot
qs.why: About sixty percent preferred a park, and overall “most of the town wanted green space.” The skateboard place and benches were single people’s ideas.

why: 'overall' is taught as an adjective; text used it as a sentence adverb. Now used as an adjective. Also removed the real town name Riverton (several real towns, some with stations) from an invented event.

set.text: Sam and Theo are twins, but they live very different lives. Sam lives in a rural area, on a farm with cows and an old red barn. The nearest store is twenty minutes away by car. Theo chose the opposite kind of life. He lives in an urban area, in an apartment on the tenth floor, and he can walk to work, shops, and three movie theaters. The brothers live five hundred miles apart, but they talk on the phone every Sunday. Sam generally gets up at five to feed the animals, while Theo sleeps until seven. Each brother says he is more comfortable where he is, and each one thinks the other is a little silly.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rural” mean?
options: in the middle of a big city
far from cities, with farms and fields
qs.why: Rural describes places far from cities, like Sam’s farm with cows. “In a big city” describes Theo’s urban life, the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “apart” mean?
qs.why: Apart means separated by distance; the brothers live five hundred miles from each other.

qs.q: Which statement about the brothers is true?
options: Theo wakes up earlier than Sam
Each one wants to move to the other's home
They have not spoken in years
They stay in touch even though they live far away
They live in the same building
qs.why: They live five hundred miles apart but “talk on the phone every Sunday.” Sam, not Theo, gets up earlier.

why: 'urban apartment' is an unnatural collocation; now 'urban area', matching 'rural area'.

set.text: When Hana Sato started piano lessons at age forty, she worried that she had no talent for music. Her teacher told her that effort matters more than a natural gift. Hana practiced for twenty minutes every evening after dinner. At first, her fingers felt slow and heavy, and she frequently pressed the wrong keys. Her progress was slow, but she could hear it. After six months, she could play a simple song all the way through. She did not play it perfectly, and she still made two small mistakes, but her family clapped. Hana's goal now is to master one piece by Bach before her next birthday.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “talent” mean?
options: a natural ability to do something well
qs.why: Talent is a natural ability. Her teacher contrasts it with effort, calling talent “a natural gift.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “master” mean?
options: learn so well that she can play it easily
qs.why: To master a skill is to learn it so well you can do it easily. “A teacher of music” is a noun meaning that does not fit “to master one piece.”

qs.q: What does the passage suggest about how Hana learned?
options: She learned fast because of her natural gift
She stopped practicing after six months
Her family did not like her playing
Steady practice helped her improve even without natural talent
She can already play Bach perfectly
qs.why: She practiced every evening and made slow but real progress, showing her teacher’s point that effort matters more than talent.

why: Awkward passive ('It was not played perfectly') replaced with natural active sentence.

set.text: Last October, a severe storm hit a small town on the coast. Strong winds damaged the roofs of many houses, and one old wooden boathouse was completely destroyed. Some families had no electricity for three days. People from nearby towns drove in with trucks to help. A church group supplied hot meals twice a day, and a local store gave away water and batteries. The government also sent aid, including blankets and money to help families fix their homes. “I have never seen people work together like this,” said Rosa Díaz, who has lived in the town for forty years.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “destroyed” mean?
options: damaged so badly that it could not be fixed
qs.why: Destroyed means damaged so badly it cannot be used or fixed. The word “completely” shows it was worse than the roofs that were only damaged.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “aid” mean?
options: a person who helps a leader
help such as blankets, food, or money
qs.why: Aid is help given to people in need; here the city sent blankets and money.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Most families left the town after the storm
Many people and groups helped the town after the storm
The storm did very little harm
The town had no electricity for a month
qs.why: The passage lists help from nearby towns, a church group, a store, and the city, and Rosa says she has never seen people work together like this.

why: Port Allen is a real town (Kauai, Hawaii; also Louisiana), so a made-up storm there is a false fact; town now unnamed. 'The city' sending aid contradicted 'small town'; now 'The government' (idea option updated to match).

set.text: Grace Mensah's old car stopped working on the highway one cold morning. She paid for a tow truck to take the vehicle to a small repair shop owned by a man named Viktor, an expert who had fixed cars for thirty years. He listened to the engine and found the problem quickly. A broken belt had stopped the engine. “I can replace it today,” he said, “with a new one from my shelf.” Viktor's shop was small, but it had all the right equipment, including a lift that could raise a car off the ground. The fee for the work was one hundred and twenty dollars, which Grace thought was fair.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “fee” mean?
options: the money paid for the work
the price of a new car
a tip left on the counter
qs.why: A fee is money paid for a service; here, $120 for fixing the car.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “expert” mean?
options: a beginner who is still learning
a person who knows a lot and is very skilled
qs.why: An expert knows a lot about something. Viktor had fixed cars for thirty years and found the problem quickly.

qs.q: What was wrong with Grace's car?
qs.why: Viktor found that “a broken belt had stopped the engine.”

set.text: Carlos Mendoza wanted to open a bicycle repair shop. He had saved some money, but not enough. So he went to the bank for a loan of twenty thousand dollars. He used it to buy tools and rent a space near the university. He saw the money he spent as an investment: he hoped the shop would make money for many years. In the first year, the shop's revenue was sixty thousand dollars. After paying rent, wages, and parts, he had a little left over. Slowly, he paid back his debt to the bank. Now, after four years, the shop is successful. Its purpose has stayed the same: to keep students riding.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “revenue” mean?
options: the money left after all costs were paid
the money he owed the bank
all the money the shop took in, before costs
qs.why: Revenue is all the money a business takes in before costs. The money left over after rent, wages and parts is profit, which was only “a little.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “debt” mean?
options: money he had to pay back
money the bank gave him for free
qs.why: A debt is money you must pay back. He “paid back his debt to the bank,” the loan.

qs.q: Why did Carlos get a loan from the bank?
options: The bank asked him to open a shop
He wanted to buy a house
His savings were not enough to start the shop
He needed to pay for school
qs.why: He “had saved some money, but not enough,” so he borrowed to buy tools and rent a space.

why: 'it' was ambiguous (loan, space, or shop); made the investment (money put in) explicit, matching the card.

set.text: For many years, a lighthouse stood on a rocky island off the coast, and a keeper lived inside it. In this story, the keeper is Elias, an old man with a gray beard. His main duty was to keep the lamp burning every night, so ships would know the location of the rocks. The wind on the island was constant; it never stopped blowing. When fog came, Elias used a loud horn to signal to the ships. Previously, when there was no light, many ships had crashed there. The stone tower stood strong through a hundred storms. In the coldest winters, even the water in his barrel froze solid.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “signal” mean?
options: make a sound to tell someone something
qs.why: To signal is to make a sound, movement or sign to tell someone something; the horn warned ships in the fog. “A light on a road” is a noun meaning.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “Previously” mean?
options: at an earlier time, before then
qs.why: Previously means at an earlier time. The sentence says “before the lighthouse was built.”

qs.q: Why was a lighthouse needed on the island?
options: Elias wanted a place to live
Ships had crashed on the rocks there before
The island had no stone for houses
Fog never came to the island
The wind made ships go faster
The town needed a lamp at night
qs.why: Before the lighthouse was built, “many ships had crashed there,” and its light showed where the rocks were.

why: 'solid stone' uses solid in the 'made all of one material/strong' sense, not the card's 'firm, not liquid' sense; now 'froze solid'. Also removed redundant 'Previously, before'.

set.text: Our class visited the city museum to see its famous collection of old clocks. More than three hundred clocks were displayed in glass cases along the walls. Some were as small as a teacup, while others were taller than our teacher. The guide told us that one gold clock was the most valuable piece in the museum. It came from an era when clocks cost so much that most families could not own one. Nobody knows the exact year it was made, but experts think it is about three hundred years old. Its origin is also not certain, though the writing on it suggests it was made in France.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “era” mean?
options: a period of history known for something
qs.why: An era is a period of history known for a particular quality; here, a time when only rich families could own clocks.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “origin” mean?
options: the place where it came from
qs.why: Origin is where something comes from. The writing suggests France, but no one is sure.

qs.q: What is known about the gold clock?
options: It was made in France in a known year
Experts think it is about 300 years old, but the exact year is unknown
It is the smallest clock in the museum
It was owned by a poor family
It is taller than the teacher
qs.why: The passage says “nobody knows the exact year,” but experts think it is about three hundred years old. France is only suggested, not certain.

why: Pocket-sized timepieces are watches, not clocks; 'only rich families could own a clock' ~300 years ago is overstated (middle-class ownership was spreading), softened to a true statement.

set.text: On a bright Saturday, about fifty people met at the river near their town to clean its banks. The event was run by a small organization that cares for the local environment. Each person got gloves and a bag. In three hours, they removed more than two hundred kilograms of trash, including bottles, old tires, and fishing line. Fishing line is dangerous for birds, because it can wrap around their legs. The leader, Mei Lin, said the work has a real impact. “Five years ago, you could hardly see a heron here,” she said. “Now these big birds are widely seen along the river.” After the cleanup, everyone shared lunch under the trees.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “impact” mean?
options: the force of one thing hitting another
qs.why: Impact here means a strong effect; Mei Lin points to the birds coming back. The meaning “force of one thing hitting another” does not fit.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “removed” mean?
qs.why: Removed means took away. The volunteers took trash away from the river banks.

qs.q: What does Mei Lin suggest about the cleanups?
options: Herons are now harder to find
The river has no more trash
They have helped birds return to the river
Only five people come to them
qs.why: She says herons were hard to see five years ago but are now widely seen, showing the work has had an effect.

why: Green River is a real river (several in the US); an invented cleanup and invented heron recovery were stated as fact about it. Made generic.
